opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that web research is fundamentally a long-horizon task, and over a long horizon you're going to make mistakes. You search for the wrong thing, you land on a page that looks authoritative but isn't, you go down a rabbit hole that doesn't pan out. The question isn't whether the agent makes mistakes. It's whether it can notice and course-correct.

The traditional way people built these systems was to hand-design the workflow: break the problem into steps, have the model plan, then search, then summarize, and maybe chain a few prompts together. That works surprisingly well for demos. But it's brittle, because you as the designer have to anticipate every failure mode, and the real web is messy in ways you just can't anticipate. When something goes off the rails at step seven, the pipeline usually has no good mechanism for backing up and trying something different.

With end-to-end reinforcement learning, you're not telling the model how to do the research. You're giving it a task, letting it take actions like searching, browsing, and reading, and then rewarding it based on whether it got to a good final answer. Over many trajectories, the model learns the behaviors that lead to success, and recovery turns out to be one of the most important of them. It learns things like, "This source contradicts what I found earlier, so let me dig in," or "This search isn't productive, let me reformulate," or "I'm not confident yet, I should keep going rather than wrap up." Nobody wrote those rules down. They emerge because they're what actually leads to reward.

There's also a subtler point. When you train only on demonstrations of good behavior, the model rarely sees itself in a bad state, so it never learns what to do when it gets there. RL puts the model in its own mistakes, over and over, and it has to learn its way out. That's the kind of training signal you need if you want an agent that holds up over dozens or hundreds of steps on the open web.

So for me it's less about RL being a magic ingredient and more that it's the right tool for the problem. If the hard part of research is adapting when things don't go as planned, you want a training method that directly optimizes for getting to the right answer, however messy the path turns out to be.

r001.rationale: It describes searching for the wrong thing and reformulating when a search is unproductive, communicating that poor search outcomes can prompt the agent to change its search.

r002.rationale: It explains that end-to-end RL rewards successful research outcomes and repeatedly puts the model in its own mistakes, where it learns to recover.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core intuition is that the thing that makes web research hard isn't any one step. If you ask a model to read a page and summarize it, or to formulate a search query, those individual steps are pretty easy for frontier models now. What's hard is that a real research task is a long sequence of those steps, and the world pushes back on you along the way. You search for something and the results are junk. You click a link and the page is paywalled, or it's about something adjacent to what you wanted. You find a source that looks authoritative and then three steps later you realize it contradicts something else you found. So the question is, what does the agent do at those moments?

And what we found is that if you build these systems the way most people build them, which is prompting a model and wrapping it in some orchestration logic, maybe a planner, maybe some retry loops, the agent tends to be very brittle at exactly those moments. It'll get a bad search result and just confidently summarize it anyway. Or it'll hit a dead end and declare victory. Or it'll go into a loop issuing basically the same query over and over. The model has never actually experienced what it feels like to be three steps down a bad path and need to back out, because it was trained on single-turn data where there's no notion of a trajectory going badly.

So the argument for end-to-end RL is really that the recovery behavior is something the model has to learn from consequences. If you let the agent run the whole task, take real actions in a real browser or against a real search index, and you reward it based on whether it actually got to a correct, well-supported answer at the end, then the model gets credit for the things that matter, which include noticing that a source is bad, deciding to try a different angle, cross-checking a claim. And it gets penalized for the failure modes I mentioned. You're not hand-coding "if the page is empty, try again," you're letting the model discover that trying again, or trying something different, is what leads to the reward.

The other piece that I think is underappreciated is that the mistakes compound. In a twenty-step task, a small error at step four changes what the model sees at steps five through twenty. If you train on individual steps in isolation, with supervised data, the distribution the model sees at training time is a bunch of clean, on-track states. But at inference time it's constantly off-track in ways it's never seen. RL on the full trajectory is the natural fix for that, because the model generates its own mistakes during training and then has to learn to deal with them. The training distribution actually matches the mess it'll encounter in deployment.

I'd also say there's a practical reason we landed here, which is that we tried the other things first. We tried a lot of prompt engineering, we tried heavier scaffolding around the model, and you can squeeze out gains, but you end up with this big pile of special cases, and every new failure mode is another patch. At some point you look at it and realize the model should just be making these decisions itself, and the way you get there is to train it on the actual objective.

r001.rationale: The response says search results can be junk and the agent may try a different angle, but it does not identify irrelevant results as evidence that the search terms were wrong.

r002.rationale: The response explains that training on full research trajectories exposes the agent to its own intermediate mistakes, and rewards or penalties teach it to recover from them.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that web research is a sequence of decisions, and you don’t really know whether those decisions were good until you see the final result. You might issue a query that doesn’t turn up anything useful, follow a misleading link, or spend too long pursuing a particular hypothesis. What matters is whether you can recognize that and change course.

If you train only on demonstrations of successful research, you mostly show the model what to do when everything goes right. You don’t necessarily teach it what to do in the states it reaches after making its own mistakes. With end-to-end reinforcement learning, the agent can experience those situations and get rewarded for ultimately producing a good answer—including when getting there requires backing up, reformulating a query, or checking a claim against another source.

So the goal isn’t to make every individual action perfect. It’s to learn a policy that can still succeed when some of its actions aren’t. Of course, that depends on the reward actually capturing research quality, rather than just whether the final answer sounds convincing.

r001.rationale: The response mentions an unhelpful query and reformulating it, but does not say that irrelevant results are evidence the search terms were wrong.

r002.rationale: It explains that end-to-end reinforcement learning lets the agent experience situations after its own mistakes and rewards eventual success, including recovering by backing up or reformulating a query.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that a mistake doesn’t necessarily have to end the task. A research agent might run a search that turns out to be unhelpful, follow the wrong link, or form a hypothesis that the next source contradicts. What matters is whether it can recognize that and change course.

With end-to-end reinforcement learning, you’re rewarding the outcome of the whole research process. That gives the model an incentive to learn recovery behaviors—trying a different query, revisiting an assumption, or looking for corroborating evidence—when those behaviors help it produce a better answer.

If you only train on demonstrations of successful trajectories, the model may learn what to do when everything goes well, but have much less guidance once it gets off track. Letting it experience those situations and learn which actions lead back to a good result is a big part of making these agents robust.

r001.rationale: It mentions an unhelpful search, but does not connect that result to the agent having chosen the wrong search terms.

r002.rationale: It explains that rewarding the outcome of the whole research process incentivizes recovery behaviors and says agents can experience off-track situations and learn which actions lead back to a good result.
